value.overview: The Green Honeycreeper is a striking tanager of humid tropical forests in the Americas. Adult males are turquoise-green with a contrasting black hood and bright yellow bill, while females are mostly green and less boldly marked. It is the only species in the genus Chlorophanes. The species often travels through forest edges and fruiting trees, where it may join mixed feeding flocks with other tanagers, honeycreepers, and euphonias.
value.classification: The Green Honeycreeper belongs to the tanager family, Thraupidae, in the order Passeriformes. Its scientific name is Chlorophanes spiza, and it is the only living species in its genus.
value.identification: The male is unmistakable in good light: vivid blue-green or turquoise-green plumage contrasts with a black head and throat, and the bill is bright yellow. Females are green overall, usually with a paler underside and a yellowish lower bill. The bill is short, stout, and slightly curved. Compared with the female Red-legged Honeycreeper, the female Green Honeycreeper is larger, more uniformly green, and has grayish rather than red legs. Immature males gradually develop the adult male pattern.
value.rangeHabitat: The Green Honeycreeper ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and central South America, including Trinidad. In Costa Rica it is a resident species, occurring mainly in humid lowland and foothill forests, forest borders, second growth, plantations, gardens, and river-edge vegetation. It is recorded on both Caribbean and Pacific slopes, although it is generally associated with wetter habitats. It can occur from the lowlands into foothill areas, locally reaching middle elevations where suitable forest remains.
value.migrationStatus: The species is generally non-migratory. In Costa Rica, Green Honeycreepers are present year-round rather than being regular seasonal migrants, although local movements may follow fruit availability and flowering or fruiting conditions.
value.breeding: Green Honeycreepers are believed to breed in pairs and construct a small, open cup nest, usually placed among foliage in a tree or shrub. The female normally performs much of the nest building and incubation, while both adults may participate in caring for the young. Breeding timing varies across the broad range and is influenced by local rainfall and food conditions. In Costa Rica, nesting is associated with humid forest and other habitats that provide dense vegetation and reliable fruit resources.
value.dietFeeding: Fruit is an important part of the diet, including small berries and fruits from forest trees, shrubs, and cultivated plants. The species also takes nectar and probably small arthropods, especially when feeding young. It forages at various levels of vegetation, often searching through leafy branches and visiting fruiting trees. Green Honeycreepers may feed alone, in pairs, or in mixed-species flocks with other tanagers, honeycreepers, and euphonias.
value.behavior: This active canopy and edge-dweller often moves quickly through foliage while feeding. It may pause upright on exposed branches but usually remains among leaves and fruiting vegetation. Pairs are common, and individuals may associate with mixed feeding flocks. The species is capable of short local movements between forest patches, gardens, and plantations. Its bright plumage makes males conspicuous, while females can be harder to detect because their green coloration blends with foliage.

conservation.populationTrend: No reliably documented global population trend is available here.
